ety.text: From Middle English lyoun, lion, leon, borrowed from Old French lion, from Latin leō, (accusative: leōnem), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), of unclear origin. Doublet of Leo, leu, lev, and Lyon. Displaced Old English lēo, from the same Latin source.

senses.d: A big cat, Panthera leo, native to Africa, India and formerly much of Europe.
ex: Tigers and lions share a common ancestor from a few million years ago.
Sinibaldus lists lion's fat as a popular medieval aphrodisiac treatment.

senses.d: A male lion, as opposed to a lioness, which is characterized by having a flowing shaggy mane and taking little part in hunting, which can be done cooperatively.
Any of various extant and extinct big cats, especially the mountain lion.
A person who shows attributes associated with the lion, such as strength, courage, or ferocity.
A famous person regarded with interest and curiosity.
ex: Such society was far more enjoyable than that of Edinburgh, for here he was not a lion, but a man.
The men were delighted to go, and became the lions of the following season in Adelaide.

senses.d: A light brown color that resembles the fur of a lion.
An old Scottish coin, with a lion on the obverse, worth 74 shillings.
Of the light brown color that resembles the fur of a lion.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French lyon, from Old French lion, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin leōnem, from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn).
Ancient Greek λέων (léōn)bor. Latin leōnem Spanish león Inherited from Latin leōnem. Doublet of leu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leon (“lion”), from Latin leōnem (“lion”), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn). Doublet of leu. Cognate with Galician and Spanish león among others.
